decks.title: Human Capital Formation in India — Part 1: Human Capital and Development
goals: Explain human capital, human capital formation and how human capital differs from physical capital
Explain the five sources of human capital formation with Indian examples
Analyse the two-way link between human capital and economic growth
Distinguish human capital from human development and assess India as a knowledge economy

slides.heading: Human Capital Formation in India
slides.body_md: Part 1: what **human capital** is, how it is **formed**, and why it matters for **growth** and **development**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: what human capital is, its five sources, how it differs from physical capital, its link with growth, human development and the knowledge economy
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Think of two farmers with the same land and the same tractor. One has learnt about soil testing and new seeds; the other has not. Who will grow more? In this chapter we look at the skills, knowledge and health inside people, which economists call human capital, and at how a country builds it.

slides.heading: What is human capital?
slides.body_md: **Human capital** is the stock of **skill, knowledge, expertise and health** embodied in the people of a country at a point of time.

rows: Outside people; can be sold separately
Inside people; goes wherever they go

visual.alt: Table comparing physical capital (machines, tools, buildings, roads; can be sold separately) with human capital (skill, knowledge, expertise, good health; lives inside people)
visual.caption: Both raise output; only one is built into people.

slides.narration: Just as a country has a stock of machines and buildings, called physical capital, it has a stock of skills and knowledge in its people, called human capital. An engineer, a nurse or a skilled weaver carries this capital wherever they go. It cannot be seen or sold separately from the person, but it raises what that person can produce.

slides.heading: Human capital formation
slides.body_md: **Human capital formation** is the **process** of adding to the stock of human capital over time.
bullets: Stock: skills and knowledge of all people at a point of time.
Process: spending on education, health, training, migration and information.
It turns a large population into a **productive asset** instead of a burden.
slides.narration: Human capital is a stock; human capital formation is the process of adding to it over time. A country with many people but little education and poor health has a large population, not a large stock of human capital. When it invests in schools, clinics and training, those same people become a productive asset. That is the central idea of this chapter.

slides.heading: Five sources of human capital

visual.alt: Flow listing the five sources of human capital formation: education, health, on-the-job training, migration and information
visual.caption: Five sources of human capital formation

slides.narration: There are five main sources of human capital formation: education, health, on-the-job training, migration and information. In the next few slides we take each in turn. For every source, ask the same question: does this spending raise the ability of a person to produce, or the return that person gets from the skills already held?

slides.heading: Education as an investment
slides.body_md: Individuals and governments spend on education today because it brings **higher earnings and output later**.

rows: Higher earnings over a working life
A family pays for a daughter's nursing diploma
A salaried job and a better standard of living
More productive workers and more tax revenue

visual.alt: Table pairing spending on education with returns: fees and time bring higher lifetime earnings; a nursing diploma brings a salaried job; public spending on schools brings more productive workers
visual.caption: Education is treated as an investment because the return comes later.

slides.narration: Why do families spend on fees, books and coaching? Because they expect higher earnings in future. In that sense education is an investment, just like buying a machine. The government also spends on schools and colleges, expecting a more productive workforce. Notice that the return comes years later, which is one reason why poor families find it hard to invest on their own.

slides.heading: Quick check: which is not a source?
slides.body_md: Which of these does **not** add to human capital?
slides.narration: For each option, ask whether it builds skills and health in people, or whether it adds to the stock of machines.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: is a course worth it?
slides.body_md: An imagined tailor in Surat pays ₹24,000 for a fashion-stitching course. Her earnings rise from ₹6,000 to ₹9,000 a month.
bullets: Step 1: Extra earnings a month = 9,000 − 6,000 = **₹3,000**.
Step 2: Months to repay = 24,000 ÷ 3,000 = **8 months**.
Step 3: Over five years, net gain = 3,000 × 12 × 5 − 24,000 = **₹1,56,000**.
Step 4: Conclude: the course is a sound investment in her human capital.

slides.narration: Let us treat a course as an investment. The tailor earns three thousand rupees more each month after the course. The course cost twenty four thousand rupees, so it pays for itself in eight months. After that, the extra income keeps coming for years. Over five years her net gain is more than one and a half lakh rupees. This is exactly why education and training are called investments.

slides.heading: Health as a source
slides.body_md: A healthy worker can work **longer and better**. Health spending includes:

rows: Treatment in a hospital when ill
Clean drinking water and good sanitation

visual.alt: Table of kinds of health spending: preventive medicine such as immunisation, curative medicine such as hospital treatment, social medicine such as health literacy, and basic facilities such as clean water and sanitation

slides.narration: A sick worker loses days of work and works with less energy. So spending on health raises the productive capacity of people. It takes several forms: preventive medicine such as vaccination, curative medicine when people fall ill, social medicine that spreads health literacy, and basic facilities like clean water and sanitation. All of these add to human capital.

slides.heading: On-the-job training
slides.body_md: Firms train their workers at the workplace, or send them for courses, to raise productivity.
bullets: Example: a car maker in Chennai trains new workers to operate welding robots.
The firm expects the **extra output** to exceed the cost of training.
Firms often ask trained workers to **stay for a period** so that the firm gains the return.
slides.narration: Much learning happens at work. A firm may train its workers on the shop floor under a skilled supervisor, or send them for a course. Training costs money, so the firm expects the extra output of trained workers to be worth more. That is why firms often ask trained workers to stay for some years; otherwise a rival firm would gain from the training.

slides.heading: Migration and information
columns:
**Migration**

People move to where their skills earn more: a nurse from Kerala to Delhi, an engineer abroad. It counts only if the **returns exceed the costs** of moving.

**Information**

Knowing about **job openings, wages and courses** helps people choose the right education and the job that uses their skills best.

rows: Higher earnings for the same skill
Higher cost of living in cities
New skills picked up at work
Money sent home to the family

visual.alt: Table of the costs of migration (transport, higher cost of living, living away from family) and its returns (higher earnings, new skills, money sent home)
visual.caption: Migration adds to human capital only when the returns exceed the costs.

slides.narration: Migration and information are the last two sources. When a skilled person moves to a place where the same skill earns more, the return on human capital rises. But migration has costs, such as transport, a higher cost of living and living away from family. It is a source only if the gain is larger. Information about jobs and courses helps people make these choices well.

slides.heading: Quick check: migration
slides.body_md: Is a nurse who moves to a better-paid hospital adding to human capital formation?
slides.narration: Think about returns and costs: does the move raise what her existing skills earn?

slides.heading: Worked example 2: should Anil migrate?
slides.body_md: Anil earns ₹10,000 a month at home and could earn ₹25,000 in a city, where living costs ₹5,000 a month more. Moving costs ₹30,000 once.
bullets: Step 1: Subtract the extra living cost and the home income from the city income.
Step 2: Multiply by 12 for a year.
Step 3: Subtract the one-time cost of moving.
Step 4: A positive result means the move adds to the return on his skills.

rows: Positive net gain, so moving pays

visual.alt: Table of the migration worked example: net extra income of 10,000 rupees a month gives 1,20,000 in a year; after the moving cost of 30,000 the first-year gain is 90,000 rupees

slides.narration: Here is how to weigh migration. In the city Anil earns more, but he must pay more for rent and food, so his net extra income is ten thousand rupees a month. Over a year that is one lakh twenty thousand rupees. Take away the one-time cost of moving, thirty thousand rupees, and he still gains ninety thousand rupees in the first year. So migration adds to the returns on his human capital.

slides.heading: Human capital vs physical capital
columns:
**Physical capital**

Tangible; can be sold; owner and capital can be separated; benefits mainly the owner.

**Human capital**

Intangible; cannot be separated from the person; less mobile across countries; benefits the owner **and society**.

rows: To the owner and to society

visual.alt: Table comparing physical and human capital on nature, separability, mobility, depreciation and benefits: physical capital is tangible, separable, fairly mobile, wears out and benefits its owner; human capital is intangible, inseparable, less mobile, ages or becomes outdated and benefits society as well

slides.narration: Both kinds of capital raise output, but they differ. A machine is tangible and can be sold, while skill stays inside a person. Physical capital moves fairly easily between countries; people face visas and cultural barriers. Both depreciate: machines wear out, while skills become outdated as technology changes. And human capital spreads benefits to society, for example when an educated mother keeps her family healthier.

slides.heading: Quick check: payback of a course
slides.body_md: Calculate how many months a course takes to pay for itself.
slides.narration: Find the extra monthly earnings first, then divide the cost of the course by that amount.

slides.narration: Human capital raises growth. Educated and healthy workers are more productive, they invent and adapt new technology, and they make better use of machines. Growth, in turn, raises incomes, so families and governments can spend more on schools and hospitals, building more human capital. Because each feeds the other, the link is two way, and it is hard to say which comes first.

slides.heading: Human capital vs human development
slides.body_md: **Human development** is the wider idea: education and health matter **for their own sake**.

visual.alt: Table comparing human capital, which sees education and health as means to raise productivity, with human development, which sees them as ends in themselves and is the wider idea

slides.narration: Human capital sees education and health as means to an end: they matter because they raise productivity. Human development sees them as ends in themselves. Being able to read, and living a long and healthy life, are part of well-being even if they add nothing to output. So a child with a disability deserves education whether or not it raises national income. Human development is the broader concept.

slides.heading: Quick check: two ideas compared
slides.body_md: How does human development differ from human capital?
slides.narration: Remember the key words: means and ends.

slides.heading: India as a knowledge economy?
slides.body_md: A **knowledge economy** grows mainly by creating and using knowledge.
bullets: **Strengths:** a large young workforce; a strong record in IT and software services.
**Gaps:** many workers have little schooling or training; research spending is limited.
**Condition:** quality education and skills must reach the majority, not just a few.
slides.narration: India's success in software and IT services has led many to say it can become a knowledge economy, where growth comes from skills and ideas rather than natural resources. There are real strengths, such as a large young workforce. But much of the workforce still has little schooling or training. The potential will be realised only if quality education and skills reach most people.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

nodes.label: Human capital: skills, knowledge and health in people
Formed by education, health, training, migration and information
Raises productivity and growth; growth funds more of it
Human development: well-being as an end

visual.alt: Summary flow of Part 1: human capital is skill, knowledge and health in people; it is formed by five sources; it raises growth and growth funds more of it; human development values well-being as an end
visual.caption: Part 1 in four lines

slides.narration: Let us sum up. Human capital is the skill, knowledge and health in people. It is formed through education, health, on-the-job training, migration and information. It differs from physical capital, and it has a two-way link with growth. Human development goes further and values education and health for their own sake.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Define human capital as a **stock** and human capital formation as a **process**.
For sources, give **all five** and an example for each.
In difference questions, state **both sides** on the same basis.
For migration, mention **costs and returns**; it counts only if returns exceed costs.
Human capital vs human development: **means vs ends**.
Numericals: show the **steps** (extra earnings, payback, net gain) with units.
slides.narration: A few tips. Keep the stock and process distinction clear. List all five sources with examples. In difference questions, write both sides on the same basis, such as tangibility. For migration, always mention costs as well as returns. For human development, the key words are means and ends. And in numericals, show each step with units to earn the step marks.

decks.title: Human Capital Formation in India — Part 2: Growth of the Education Sector
goals: Explain why the government provides and regulates education and health
Interpret the two indicators of government spending on education and the 6 per cent goal
Explain the right to education under Article 21A and the RTE Act 2009
Evaluate the achievements and problems of the education sector in India

slides.heading: Growth of the Education Sector in India
slides.body_md: Part 2: how India spends on education, what the **right to education** means, and how far we have come.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: why the State steps in, measuring education spending, the 6 per cent goal, the right to education, achievements and problems, and the way forward
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: In Part 2 we look at India's record. Why does the government run schools at all? How do we measure its spending? What does the right to education promise? And, honestly, how well has the education sector done so far, and what still needs to change?

slides.heading: Why the State steps in
slides.body_md: Education and health are not left only to the market, for four reasons.

headers: What goes wrong without the State
rows: Returns come years later; poor families cannot pay now
Private choices ignore benefits to others
Families cannot judge quality; some providers overcharge
The poor are shut out of schools and hospitals

visual.alt: Table of reasons for State provision of education and health: long gestation, social benefits, information gaps and equity, with what goes wrong without the State

slides.narration: Education and health bring returns over many years, and poor families cannot pay the cost today. They also benefit society, which private choices ignore. Families often cannot judge the quality of a school or a hospital, and some providers overcharge. And without public provision the poor would be shut out. So central and state governments, along with private providers, all play a part.

slides.heading: Measuring government spending on education
slides.body_md: Two indicators are used.

rows: Education spending as a share of total government expenditure
How high education ranks among the government's priorities
Education spending as a share of GDP
How much of the country's income goes to education

visual.alt: Table of the two indicators of education spending: share of total government expenditure shows priority; share of GDP shows how much of national income goes to education

slides.narration: There are two ways to judge government spending on education. The first is its share in total government expenditure, which tells us how high education ranks among the government's priorities. The second is its share in GDP, which tells us how much of the country's income is devoted to education. A government can score well on one and poorly on the other.

slides.heading: The 6 per cent goal
slides.body_md: The **Education Commission (1964–66)** recommended public spending on education of about **6 per cent of GDP**; the **National Education Policy 2020** repeated the goal.

slides.narration: In the nineteen sixties, the Education Commission, often called the Kothari Commission, recommended that public spending on education should reach about six per cent of GDP. The National Education Policy of twenty twenty repeated this goal. Actual public spending in India has remained below it. The chart shows an imagined state that falls short in the same way.

slides.heading: Quick check: six per cent of what?
slides.body_md: Does the 6 per cent goal refer to the government budget or to GDP?
slides.narration: Look again at the two indicators. Which one compares spending with the size of the economy?

slides.heading: Worked example 1: one state, two indicators
slides.body_md: Imagined Tapti Pradesh: State Domestic Product ₹2,50,000 crore, total spending ₹50,000 crore, education ₹8,000 crore.
bullets: Step 1: Share of government expenditure = **16%**, a high priority.
Step 2: Share of State Domestic Product = **3.2%**, below the 6 per cent goal.
Step 3: Spending at 6 per cent = ₹15,000 crore; extra needed = **₹7,000 crore**.
Step 4: Conclude: education is a priority in the budget, but the budget itself is small relative to income.

visual.alt: Table of the worked example: education spending of 8,000 crore is 16 per cent of government expenditure and 3.2 per cent of State Domestic Product; reaching 6 per cent needs 15,000 crore, or 7,000 crore more

slides.narration: Let us apply both indicators to an imagined state. Education takes sixteen per cent of the state's spending, which looks like a high priority. But it is only three point two per cent of the state's income, about half of the six per cent goal. To reach the goal, the state must spend seven thousand crore rupees more. So both claims, priority and shortfall, can be true at once.

slides.heading: The right to education
slides.body_md: Elementary education is a **fundamental right**.

rows: Article 21A: free and compulsory education for ages 6–14
Law that gives effect to it
Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009
Every child can be admitted to a school near home
Private unaided schools reserve 25 per cent of entry-level seats
Norms for teachers, classrooms and facilities

visual.alt: Table of the right to education: Article 21A gives free and compulsory education for ages 6 to 14; the RTE Act 2009 gives effect to it with neighbourhood schools, 25 per cent of entry seats in private unaided schools for weaker sections, and norms for teachers and facilities

slides.narration: Article 21A of the Constitution makes free and compulsory education a fundamental right for every child aged six to fourteen. The Right to Education Act of two thousand and nine gives effect to this right. Children can be admitted to a neighbourhood school, private unaided schools must keep a quarter of their entry seats for children from weaker sections, and schools must meet norms for teachers and facilities.

slides.heading: Quick check: age group
slides.body_md: Which age group does Article 21A cover?
slides.narration: Recall the ages for which elementary education is free and compulsory.

slides.heading: Achievements
slides.body_md: India has made large gains in **access** to education.

rows: From under one in five people (1951) to about three in four (Census 2011)
Help keep poor children in school
A large system of universities, institutes and colleges

visual.alt: Table of achievements: literacy rose from under one in five people in 1951 to about three in four in 2011; primary enrolment is close to universal; midday meals and free books help retention; higher and technical education has grown
visual.caption: Broad, rounded statements; check current figures in your textbook.

slides.narration: Since independence, literacy has risen from fewer than one in five people to about three in four by the census of twenty eleven. Enrolment in primary school is now close to universal, helped by midday meals and free textbooks. India has also built a very large system of higher and technical education, which supplies doctors, engineers and other skilled workers.

slides.heading: Problems that remain
slides.body_md: Gains in access have not been matched by gains in **quality and equity**.

rows: Children finish classes without basic reading and arithmetic
Large differences between states and between rural and urban areas
Many leave after the elementary stage
Public spending below the 6 per cent of GDP goal
Skills lost abroad or left idle at home

sections.heading: 1. Human capital and human capital formation
sections.body_md:
**Human capital** is the stock of skill, knowledge, expertise and health embodied in the people of a country at a point of time. **Human capital formation** is the process of adding to this stock over time by spending on education, health, training, migration and information.

A large population becomes a productive **asset** only when it has human capital; otherwise it can be a burden on scarce resources.

key_terms.definition_md: The stock of skill, knowledge and health in a country's people at a point of time.
The process of increasing the stock of human capital over time.

sections.heading: 2. Sources of human capital formation
sections.body_md:
1. **Education:** spending on schooling and higher studies raises future earnings and output; it is an investment because the return comes later.
2. **Health:** preventive medicine (immunisation), curative medicine (treatment), social medicine (health literacy), clean water and sanitation raise the capacity to work.
3. **On-the-job training:** firms train workers at the workplace or send them for courses, expecting extra output; they often bind trained workers to stay for a period.
4. **Migration:** moving to where skills earn more (rural to urban, or abroad); it counts only if the returns exceed the costs (transport, higher cost of living, psychic costs).
5. **Information:** spending on information about jobs, wages, education and health helps people make better choices.

key_terms.definition_md: Training given by firms to their workers at or for the workplace.
Health measures that stop disease before it occurs, such as vaccination.

sections.heading: 3. Human capital and physical capital
sections.body_md:
- **Nature:** physical capital is tangible; human capital is intangible.
- **Separability:** a machine can be sold apart from its owner; skill cannot be separated from the person.
- **Mobility:** physical capital moves fairly easily between countries; people face restrictions of nationality and culture.
- **Depreciation:** machines wear out; skills become outdated, and people age, so continuous learning is needed.
- **Benefits:** physical capital mainly benefits its owner; human capital also creates **social benefits** (an educated person helps others learn and stay healthy).

The two are **complements**: modern machinery needs trained people to run it.

key_terms.definition_md: A benefit that reaches people other than the one who paid for the good or service.

sections.heading: 4. Human capital, growth and human development
sections.body_md:
**Growth:** human capital raises labour productivity, encourages innovation and helps the economy use physical capital well. Higher growth in turn gives families and governments more to spend on schools and hospitals. The link is **two-way**, and it is hard to show which comes first.

**Human development** treats education and health as **ends in themselves**, part of well-being; human capital treats them as **means** to raise productivity. Human development is the wider idea.

**Knowledge economy:** India's IT and software services show the potential of a skilled workforce, but much of the workforce still has little schooling or training; quality education for the majority is the condition for this potential to be realised.

An economy whose growth comes mainly from creating, spreading and using knowledge.
The emigration of highly skilled people, so that the home country loses the return on their training.

sections.heading: 5. Government and education spending in India
sections.body_md:
**Why the State intervenes:** returns come over a long period and poor families cannot pay now; education and health have social benefits; families face information gaps and may be overcharged; and equity requires that the poor are not shut out. Education is on the concurrent list, so both the Centre and the states are responsible; private institutions also provide it.

**Indicators:** education expenditure as a percentage of (i) total government expenditure, which shows priority, and (ii) GDP, which shows how much of national income goes to education.

**Goal:** the **Education Commission (1964–66)** recommended about **6 per cent of GDP**; the **National Education Policy 2020** repeated it. Public spending has remained below this level.

**Right to education:** **Article 21A** makes free and compulsory education for children aged **6 to 14** a fundamental right; the **RTE Act 2009** gives effect to it (neighbourhood schools, 25 per cent of entry-level seats in private unaided schools for weaker sections, norms for teachers and facilities).

sections.heading: 6. Achievements, problems and the way forward
sections.body_md:
**Achievements (broad):** literacy has risen from under one in five people in 1951 to about three in four (Census 2011); primary enrolment is close to universal; midday meals and free textbooks help keep poor children in school; a large system of higher and technical education has grown.

**Problems:** low quality of learning; gender gap (female literacy below male literacy); regional and rural–urban gaps; dropouts after the elementary stage; public spending below the 6 per cent goal; brain drain; unemployment among educated youth.

**Way forward:** raise public spending towards 6 per cent of GDP; train and support teachers; measure learning outcomes, not only enrolment; link vocational education to jobs; focus on girls and lagging regions.

questions.stem_md: **Human capital** refers to

options.text_md: the total population of a country at a point of time
the stock of skill, knowledge and health embodied in the people of a country
machines and buildings owned by workers
the money saved by households in banks

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** the stock of skill, knowledge and health embodied in the people of a country. Human capital is the stock of productive ability (skill, expertise, knowledge, health) in people. Population is a head count, machines are physical capital, and savings are financial assets.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is **NOT** a source of human capital formation?

options.text_md: Expenditure on vocational training
Expenditure on health care
Migration in search of better-paid work
Buying a new tractor for a farm

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Buying a new tractor for a farm. A tractor is physical capital. Training, health and migration all raise the productive ability or earnings of people, so they are sources of human capital.

questions.stem_md: Human capital formation is best described as

options.text_md: the process of adding to the stock of human capital over time
the total number of educated people in a country on a given date
the transfer of workers from villages to cities
the purchase of shares in companies by households

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** the process of adding to the stock of human capital over time. Human capital is a stock; human capital formation is the process (a flow over time) of adding to that stock through education, health, training and so on.

questions.stem_md: Which statement correctly distinguishes human capital from physical capital?

options.text_md: Physical capital is intangible, whereas human capital is tangible
Only human capital depreciates with time
Human capital cannot be separated from its owner, whereas physical capital can be sold apart from its owner
Physical capital is perfectly mobile between countries, while human capital never moves

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Human capital cannot be separated from its owner, whereas physical capital can be sold apart from its owner. Skill stays with the person who owns it, while a machine can be sold separately. Physical capital is tangible and human capital intangible; both depreciate (skills become outdated); and both can move, though under different restrictions.

questions.stem_md: A software firm in Pune pays for its new engineers to attend a six-week course on cloud security and asks them to stay with the firm for two years afterwards. Why does the firm insist on the two-year condition?

options.text_md: Because the law forbids trained workers from changing jobs
Because training lowers the productivity of workers in the short run
To recover the benefit of the extra productivity created by the training it paid for
To avoid paying the trainees any salary during the course

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** To recover the benefit of the extra productivity created by the training it paid for. On-the-job training is an investment by the firm; it gains only if the trained worker stays long enough for its extra output to repay the cost. No law forbids changing jobs, and training raises productivity.

questions.stem_md: Sunil moves from a village in Bihar to Bengaluru for a job in a hotel. Which of the following is a **cost** of this migration?

options.text_md: Higher cost of living in the city and the cost of transport
The higher salary he earns in Bengaluru
The skills he picks up at the hotel
The money he sends back to his family

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Higher cost of living in the city and the cost of transport. Migration costs include transport and the higher cost of living (and psychic costs of living away). Higher earnings and new skills are the returns that justify the move.

questions.stem_md: A state sets up a free portal that lists job openings, required skills and training centres. This spending adds to human capital mainly because

options.text_md: it directly increases the stock of machines in the state
it reduces the population of the state
it guarantees a government job to every user
information helps people choose the education and jobs that make the best use of their abilities

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** information helps people choose the education and jobs that make the best use of their abilities. Spending on information about labour markets and education helps people decide what to learn and where to work, raising the returns to their human capital. It adds no machines, does not change population, and guarantees nothing.

questions.stem_md: Which statement best describes the link between human capital and economic growth?

options.text_md: Only economic growth affects human capital; the reverse never happens
It runs both ways: more human capital raises output, and higher incomes allow more spending on education and health
Human capital raises growth only in agriculture
There is no link, because growth depends only on physical capital

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** It runs both ways: more human capital raises output, and higher incomes allow more spending on education and health. Educated, healthy workers are more productive and innovate, which raises growth; a richer economy can in turn spend more on schools, hospitals and training. Physical capital alone cannot explain growth.

questions.stem_md: How does **human development** differ from **human capital**?

options.text_md: Human development treats education and health as ends in themselves; human capital treats them as means to raise productivity
Human development is concerned only with incomes; human capital only with health
The two terms mean exactly the same thing
Human capital is a wider idea than human development

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Human development treats education and health as ends in themselves; human capital treats them as means to raise productivity. Human capital values education and health for the extra output they produce; human development values them as part of well-being whether or not they raise output. Human development is therefore the wider idea.

questions.stem_md: Two weavers in an imagined Varanasi workshop use the same loom. Meera has completed a course in pattern design and produces saris that sell for much more. The difference in their earnings is mainly due to

options.text_md: physical capital
human capital
land
financial capital

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** human capital. Both use the same physical capital (the loom); Meera's extra skill from the design course is human capital, which raises the value of her output.

questions.stem_md: An economy in which growth comes mainly from the creation, spread and use of knowledge, for example through information technology, is called a

options.text_md: subsistence economy
closed economy
knowledge economy
barter economy

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** knowledge economy. A knowledge economy relies on skilled people and information technology. A subsistence economy produces only for survival, a closed economy has no foreign trade, and a barter economy has no money.

questions.stem_md: Many doctors and engineers trained at public expense in India go abroad and settle there. From India's point of view, this is a problem mainly because

options.text_md: it increases India's population
it lowers wages in the countries they move to
it raises the number of seats in Indian medical colleges
the country loses the returns on human capital that it paid to create

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** the country loses the returns on human capital that it paid to create. This is brain drain: public money creates scarce skills, but the output those skills produce is lost to the home economy. Population does not rise, and effects abroad are not India's concern here.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is an example of **preventive** health spending?

options.text_md: Surgery for a broken leg in a district hospital
Treating a patient with malaria
Buying medicines for a patient with tuberculosis
A child immunisation drive in an imagined tribal block of Odisha

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A child immunisation drive in an imagined tribal block of Odisha. Preventive medicine (immunisation) stops illness before it occurs. Surgery and treating malaria or TB are curative medicine.

questions.stem_md: Why is human capital formation said to be necessary for **using physical capital well**?

options.text_md: Human capital is a substitute that removes the need for any machines
Physical capital can only be bought by educated people
Modern machines need trained engineers, technicians and managers to run and maintain them
Educated people do not need machines

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Modern machines need trained engineers, technicians and managers to run and maintain them. Physical and human capital are complements: imported or modern machinery is wasted without people trained to operate, repair and improve it.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Human capital is intangible.

**Reason (R):** Human capital is built into the minds and bodies of people and cannot be seen or sold separately from them.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both statements are true and R explains A: skill and knowledge exist only inside people, which is why human capital is intangible.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Expenditure on health is a source of human capital formation.

**Reason (R):** A healthy worker can work longer and more productively than a sick one.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R is the reason: health raises the productive capacity of a worker, which is the essence of human capital.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Human capital, unlike physical capital, never depreciates.

**Reason (R):** Skills can become outdated as technology changes, so workers need continuous training.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A is false: human capital depreciates with age and as skills become outdated. R is true, and in fact shows why A is false.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Human development is a broader concept than human capital.

**Reason (R):** Education and health raise labour productivity.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both are true, but R does not explain A. R states the human capital view (education raises productivity); A is true because human development values education and health even when they do not raise output.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The benefits of human capital go only to the person who owns it.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** Human capital has social benefits too: an educated, healthy person spreads knowledge, keeps the family healthier and raises the productivity of others around them.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A nurse who moves from Kerala to a hospital in Delhi because she can earn more is adding to human capital formation through migration.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** Migration that lets a person use her skills where they earn more raises the returns to her human capital, so it is counted as a source of human capital formation, as long as the gain exceeds the cost of moving.

questions.stem_md: Training given by a firm to its own workers at the workplace is called ___ training.
questions.solution_md: Training given by firms to their employees at the workplace is on-the-job training.

questions.stem_md: Match each imagined case with the source of human capital formation it shows.

options.text_md: A dairy cooperative runs a two-day course on cattle care for its members
A Class 12 student joins a degree course in commerce
A village gets a primary health centre and a clean water supply
A welder moves from Lucknow to Surat where shipyards pay more

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). A course for members while they work is on-the-job training; a degree is education; a health centre and clean water are health spending; moving to where skills earn more is migration.

questions.stem_md: Arrange the steps of the chain by which spending on education raises economic growth.

options.text_md: Output and incomes grow faster
Spending on schools, colleges and training
Labour productivity rises and new ideas are used
People gain knowledge and skills

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (b) → (d) → (c) → (a). Spending creates skills, skills raise productivity and innovation, and higher productivity raises output and incomes (which can then fund more education).

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: An imagined electrician course at an ITI costs ₹60,000. After it, Rahul's monthly earnings rise from ₹12,000 to ₹18,000. In how many months will the extra earnings repay the cost of the course?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Extra earnings a month = 18,000 − 12,000 = ₹6,000.
Step 2: Months to repay = 60,000 ÷ 6,000 = 10 months.

questions.stem_md: An imagined farm worker earning ₹450 a day falls ill with malaria and loses 24 working days in a year. How much income does he lose (in ₹)?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Income lost = days lost × daily wage.
Step 2: 24 × 450 = 10,800. So ₹10,800.

questions.stem_md: Anil earns ₹10,000 a month in his village. In a city he can earn ₹25,000 a month, but living there costs him ₹5,000 a month more, and moving costs ₹30,000 once. What is his net gain from migrating in the first year (in ₹)? *(Imagined figures.)*
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Net extra income a month = 25,000 − 5,000 − 10,000 = ₹10,000.
Step 2: For 12 months = 10,000 × 12 = ₹1,20,000.
Step 3: Less the one-time cost: 1,20,000 − 30,000 = 90,000. So ₹90,000.

marking_scheme.step: Net monthly gain after the extra living cost
Annual gain less the cost of moving

questions.stem_md: Give two differences between human capital and physical capital.
questions.solution_md: Any two valid bases (tangibility, separability from the owner, mobility, private versus social benefit), each stating both sides.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Tangibility:** physical capital (a machine) is **tangible** and can be sold in the market; human capital is **intangible** and stays with its owner.
2. **Benefits:** physical capital mainly benefits its **owner**; human capital also gives **social benefits** (an educated person helps others learn and stay healthy).

questions.stem_md: Explain, with an example, how health expenditure adds to human capital.
questions.solution_md: Link health to the ability to work (more days, more effort) and give a concrete example.

answer.model_answer_md: A **healthy worker** works more days and with more energy. For example, if a mason in Jaipur is vaccinated and has clean water, he **misses fewer days** to illness and lays more bricks a day, so his **productivity and earnings** rise.

marking_scheme.step: Health raises the capacity to work

questions.stem_md: Why is expenditure on information about jobs and education treated as a source of human capital formation?
questions.solution_md: Information improves decisions about what to learn and where to work, raising returns to skills.

answer.model_answer_md: Information about **job openings, wages and courses** helps people choose the **right education** and the job where their skills earn the most. Without it, skills may be wasted or people may train for jobs that no longer exist.

marking_scheme.step: Information guides choice of education and job
Better use of skills / higher returns

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between human capital and human development.
questions.solution_md: State the means-versus-ends contrast for both ideas.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Human capital** sees education and health as **means** to raise labour productivity and output.
2. **Human development** sees them as **ends in themselves**: being able to read and live a healthy life matter for well-being even if they add nothing to output.

questions.stem_md: How does human capital contribute to economic growth? Give three points.
questions.solution_md: Three distinct channels, each linked to higher output.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Productivity:** educated, trained workers produce more output per hour than untrained ones.
2. **Innovation:** skilled people create and adapt new technology, which raises output from the same resources.
3. **Absorbing capital:** a skilled workforce can run modern machines and manage firms, so investment in physical capital pays off.

marking_scheme.step: Innovation and use of new technology

questions.stem_md: Explain any three sources of human capital formation.
questions.solution_md: Any three of education, health, on-the-job training, migration and information, each explained.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Education:** schooling and higher studies build knowledge and raise future earnings.
2. **Health:** preventive and curative care, clean water and nutrition let people work longer and better.
3. **On-the-job training:** firms train workers in new methods, raising their productivity at the workplace.
(Also: migration, information.)

questions.stem_md: "India can become a knowledge economy." Give one argument for and two conditions that must be met.
questions.solution_md: A balanced answer: one strength, then two realistic conditions.

answer.model_answer_md:
**For:** India has a **large young population** and a strong record in **IT and software services**, which use skills more than natural resources.
**Conditions:** (1) **quality** schooling and higher education must reach rural and poor students, not just a few institutions; (2) **digital infrastructure** and research spending must expand so that knowledge is created here, not only applied.

questions.stem_md: Explain the role of human capital in economic growth. Why is the relationship described as two-way?
questions.solution_md: Four points on how human capital raises growth, then the reverse link from growth to human capital.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Productivity:** an educated, trained worker produces more and better output than an untrained one.
2. **Innovation:** skilled people invent and adapt technology, raising output from given resources.
3. **Physical capital:** machines yield returns only when engineers and technicians can run and maintain them.
4. **Other effects:** human capital changes attitudes (to savings, family size, hygiene), which also supports growth.
5. **Two-way link:** growth raises incomes, so families and governments can spend **more on schools and hospitals**, which builds more human capital. Each feeds the other, though it is hard to prove which comes first.

marking_scheme.step: Reverse link: growth funds human capital

questions.stem_md: Explain the five sources of human capital formation, with an Indian example of each.
questions.solution_md: Each source named, explained in a phrase and given its own Indian example.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Education:** a girl in Assam completing Class 12 can train as a nurse and earn far more.
2. **Health:** a vaccination drive in Bihar villages cuts days lost to illness.
3. **On-the-job training:** a car maker in Chennai trains new workers in robot welding.
4. **Migration:** a carpenter moves from Odisha to Hyderabad, where his skills earn more than the cost of moving.
5. **Information:** a state job portal tells youth which courses lead to jobs in demand.

questions.stem_md: Article 21A of the Constitution and the Right to Education Act 2009 make education free and compulsory for children in the age group

options.text_md: 3 to 10 years
6 to 14 years
5 to 18 years
10 to 16 years

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** 6 to 14 years. Article 21A and the RTE Act 2009 cover children aged 6 to 14 years.

questions.stem_md: The goal that public expenditure on education should reach about **6 per cent of GDP** was first set out by the

options.text_md: Education Commission of 1964–66 (Kothari Commission)
Planning Commission in 1951
Reserve Bank of India
Finance Commission in 2020

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Education Commission of 1964–66 (Kothari Commission). The Education Commission (1964–66), chaired by D. S. Kothari, recommended about 6 per cent of GDP; the National Education Policy 2020 repeated the goal.

questions.stem_md: Which indicator tells us how much the government spends on education **relative to the size of the economy**?

options.text_md: Education expenditure as a percentage of total government expenditure
Education expenditure as a percentage of GDP
The number of schools in the country
The literacy rate

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Education expenditure as a percentage of GDP. Spending as a share of GDP compares education spending with the size of the economy. Share of total government expenditure shows its priority in the budget; schools and literacy are outcome or input counts.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined district, almost every child of primary-school age is enrolled, but a survey finds that many Class 5 children cannot read a Class 2 text. This shows that

options.text_md: the district has achieved universal quality education
enrolment is the main problem in the district
children in the district do not attend any school
access has improved, but the quality of learning remains a problem

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** access has improved, but the quality of learning remains a problem. Near-universal enrolment means access is good; weak reading shows poor learning outcomes, so quality, not enrolment, is the problem.

questions.stem_md: Which measure is most directly aimed at reducing **dropouts** among children from poor families?

options.text_md: Free midday meals and free textbooks in government schools
Raising fees in government schools
Closing small village schools
Allowing children to start work at 10 years of age

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Free midday meals and free textbooks in government schools. Midday meals and free books reduce the cost of schooling and give families a reason to keep children in school. The other options raise costs or push children out.

questions.stem_md: A persistent feature of literacy in India is that

options.text_md: female literacy has always been higher than male literacy
literacy is the same in all states
female literacy has been lower than male literacy
rural literacy is higher than urban literacy

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** female literacy has been lower than male literacy. Although the gap has narrowed, female literacy has remained below male literacy, and rural literacy below urban literacy, with large differences between states.

questions.stem_md: An imagined state spends a large share of its education budget on a few universities while many village schools lack teachers. The main concern with this pattern is that

options.text_md: universities do not create any human capital
school education is the responsibility of private firms only
spending on higher education per student is high while basic schooling, which reaches far more children, is neglected
it raises the literacy rate too quickly

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** spending on higher education per student is high while basic schooling, which reaches far more children, is neglected. Higher education serves fewer students at a higher cost per student; if basic schooling is starved, most children lose out. Universities do create human capital, and schooling is mainly a public responsibility.

questions.stem_md: Unemployment among educated youth is a concern for human capital formation mainly because

options.text_md: resources spent on their education give little return when their skills are not used
educated people do not want to work
it reduces the number of schools
it lowers the literacy rate

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** resources spent on their education give little return when their skills are not used. When graduates and diploma holders find no suitable work, the human capital built at public and private cost lies idle, a waste of resources.

questions.stem_md: An imagined school has 1,200 pupils and 30 teachers. Its pupil–teacher ratio is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** 40 : 1. Pupil–teacher ratio = pupils ÷ teachers = 1,200 ÷ 30 = 40, so 40 pupils per teacher.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is a problem of **regional disparity** in education?

options.text_md: Boys and girls study the same syllabus
Literacy and school completion are much higher in some states than in others
Private schools charge fees
Universities offer many courses

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Literacy and school completion are much higher in some states than in others. Regional disparity means differences between states or regions in outcomes such as literacy and completion; the other statements describe no disparity.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The Right to Education Act 2009 made elementary education a legal entitlement.

**Reason (R):** Under Article 21A, the State must provide free and compulsory education to all children aged 6 to 14.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: the Act gives effect to the fundamental right in Article 21A, so children can claim elementary schooling as of right.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Public expenditure on education in India has stayed below the long-standing goal of 6 per cent of GDP.

**Reason (R):** Education in India is provided only by the central government.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true (spending has remained below the 6 per cent goal). R is false: education is on the concurrent list and states spend the larger share; private and aided institutions also provide it.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Educating girls has benefits beyond the income of the girl herself.

**Reason (R):** Educated women tend to have healthier children, smaller families and more say in household decisions.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: the gains spread to children's health, family size and the status of women, which is why girls' education has large social returns.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The 6 per cent goal for education refers to 6 per cent of total government expenditure.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** The goal refers to public expenditure on education as about 6 per cent of **GDP**, not of the government budget.

questions.stem_md: Free and compulsory education for children aged 6 to 14 became a fundamental right under Article ___ of the Constitution.
questions.solution_md: Article 21A, given effect by the RTE Act 2009.

questions.stem_md: Match each imagined situation with the problem of the education sector it shows.

options.text_md: Village girls leave school after Class 8 because the nearest high school is 12 km away
Children in Class 6 cannot solve Class 3 arithmetic
A district in one state has 90 per cent literacy, while a district in another has 60 per cent
Graduates queue for a few clerical posts

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(s), (b)–(q), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). Distance pushing girls out is a gender and dropout problem; weak arithmetic shows low quality; differences between districts of different states show regional disparity; graduates without suitable jobs show educated unemployment.

questions.stem_md: An imagined state has a State Domestic Product of ₹4,00,000 crore and spends ₹12,000 crore on education. What is education spending as a percentage of its State Domestic Product?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Share = education spending ÷ State Domestic Product × 100.
Step 2: 12,000 ÷ 4,00,000 × 100 = 3 per cent.

questions.stem_md: For the same imagined state (State Domestic Product ₹4,00,000 crore, education spending ₹12,000 crore), how much more must it spend each year to reach 6 per cent of its State Domestic Product (in ₹ crore)?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Spending at 6 per cent = 6 ÷ 100 × 4,00,000 = ₹24,000 crore.
Step 2: Extra needed = 24,000 − 12,000 = 12,000. So ₹12,000 crore.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined block, 400 children joined Class 1 together and 340 of them completed Class 8. What percentage of the group dropped out before completing Class 8?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Dropouts = 400 − 340 = 60.
Step 2: Dropout rate = 60 ÷ 400 × 100 = 15 per cent.

questions.stem_md: State two provisions of the Right to Education Act 2009.
questions.solution_md: Any two correct provisions of the Act.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Free and compulsory** elementary education for every child aged **6 to 14** years in a neighbourhood school.
2. Private unaided schools must reserve **25 per cent** of entry-level seats for children from weaker and disadvantaged groups. (Also: norms for teachers and buildings; no screening tests at admission.)

questions.stem_md: Name the two indicators used to judge government expenditure on education and say what each shows.
questions.solution_md: Name both indicators and give what each measures.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Education expenditure as a percentage of total government expenditure:** how high education ranks among the government's **priorities**.
2. **Education expenditure as a percentage of GDP:** how much of the country's **income** is devoted to education.

marking_scheme.step: Share of government expenditure, with meaning

questions.stem_md: Suggest two measures to reduce the dropout of girls from secondary school in rural areas.
questions.solution_md: Two practical measures that address distance, safety or cost.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Schools closer to home** or safe transport (bicycles, buses) so that distance does not end a girl's schooling.
2. **Separate toilets, women teachers and scholarships** tied to attendance, which make schooling safer and cheaper for families.

questions.stem_md: Why is vocational education important for India's human capital?
questions.solution_md: Link vocational skills to employability and productivity.

answer.model_answer_md: Vocational courses give **job-ready skills** (electrician, nurse, welder) that the economy needs. They reduce **educated unemployment** among youth who have degrees but no marketable skill, and they raise **productivity** in industry and services.

questions.stem_md: State three achievements of the education sector in India since independence.
questions.solution_md: Three distinct achievements, stated broadly.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Literacy** has risen from under one in five people at independence to about three in four (Census 2011).
2. **Enrolment** in primary school is now close to universal, helped by the RTE Act and midday meals.
3. A large network of **higher and technical institutions** (universities, IITs, medical colleges) has built skilled human capital.

marking_scheme.step: Growth of higher and technical education

questions.stem_md: Explain three problems of the education sector in India.
questions.solution_md: Three distinct problems, each explained.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Low quality:** many children complete primary school without basic reading and arithmetic.
2. **Gender and regional gaps:** girls, rural children and some states lag behind in literacy and completion.
3. **Low spending:** public expenditure has remained below the 6 per cent of GDP goal, so schools lack teachers and facilities.

questions.stem_md: Critically evaluate the state of the education sector in India.
questions.solution_md: Two achievements, two problems, and a balanced conclusion.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Access:** literacy has risen greatly and primary enrolment is close to universal; the **RTE Act 2009** made elementary education a right.
2. **Higher education:** a large system of universities and technical institutes supplies skilled workers for IT, health and industry.
3. **Quality:** learning levels are often low; many children cannot read or calculate at their class level.
4. **Equity:** girls, rural children, poorer groups and some states still lag behind; dropouts rise after the elementary stage.
5. **Judgement:** India has achieved **quantity** more than **quality**; raising spending towards **6 per cent of GDP** and focusing on teachers and learning outcomes is the next step.

marking_scheme.step: Balanced judgement with a way forward

questions.stem_md: Why should the government intervene in education and health? Explain.
questions.solution_md: Five reasons: long gestation, externalities, information, equity, legal duty.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Long-term gains:** returns to education and health come over many years, and poor families cannot wait or pay the cost now.
2. **Social benefits:** an educated, healthy person benefits others (less disease, better-informed citizens), which private choices ignore.
3. **Information gaps:** families may not know which courses or treatments are worth paying for, and private providers may overcharge.
4. **Equity:** without public schools and hospitals, the poor would be shut out and inequality would grow.
5. **Constitutional duty:** Article 21A makes elementary education a right, so the State must provide it.

questions.stem_md: Identify three problems of human capital formation in India and suggest a measure for each. Which do you consider most urgent, and why?
questions.solution_md: Three problems each paired with a realistic measure, then a reasoned choice.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Brain drain:** skilled doctors and engineers emigrate. *Measure:* better research facilities and pay at home.
2. **Poor quality of schooling:** weak learning outcomes. *Measure:* trained teachers, regular assessment of learning.
3. **Low public spending:** below 6 per cent of GDP. *Measure:* raise education and health budgets steadily.
4. **Most urgent:** the **quality of school learning**, because every later skill (higher education, training) depends on basic reading and arithmetic.
5. Without it, more spending or more seats will not create usable human capital.

questions.stem_md: India is often described as a country that can become a "knowledge economy". Examine this claim in the light of the state of its human capital.
questions.solution_md: Two strengths, two weaknesses, then a conditional conclusion.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Strength:** a large young workforce and a world-class **IT and software services** sector show that Indian skills can compete globally.
2. **Strength:** a large number of engineers and scientists graduate each year, and digital access is spreading.
3. **Weakness:** much of the workforce has **little schooling or training**, and many work in low-productivity jobs.
4. **Weakness:** quality gaps in schools and low spending on **research** limit the creation of new knowledge.
5. **Conclusion:** the potential is real, but it depends on spreading **quality education and skills** to the majority, not only to a few.

questions.stem_md: Read the passage and answer the questions that follow. *(An imagined account written by SOYL for practice; the person and figures are not real.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Step 1: Monthly rise = 18,000 − 12,000 = ₹6,000.
Step 2: Yearly rise = 6,000 × 12 = 72,000. So ₹72,000.

**(b)** Training paid for by the employer during employment is on-the-job training.

**(c) (i)** Higher returns to existing skills, plus one cost from the passage.

**OR (c) (ii)** Compare cost with the extra monthly earnings and conclude.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **₹72,000**

**(b)** **On-the-job training.**

**(c) (i)** Moving lets her **use her nursing skills where they earn more**, raising the return on her human capital, which is why migration counts as a source. **Cost:** the higher **rent** (cost of living) in Pune.

Name the source of human capital shown by the employer sending Rahul for a course on solar panels.

children.stem_md: **Either** (i): Using the passage, explain why the sister's move to Pune is a source of human capital formation, and name one cost of the move.

alternatives.solution_md: Compare cost with the extra monthly earnings and conclude.

questions.stem_md: Study the data and answer the questions that follow. *(Imagined state and figures, written by SOYL for practice.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Step 1: Share = 12,000 ÷ 80,000 × 100.
Step 2: = 15 per cent.

**(b)** Step 1: Share = 12,000 ÷ 4,00,000 × 100.
Step 2: = 3 per cent.

**(c) (i)** Each side relies on a different indicator; compare the second with the 6 per cent goal.
